posts.name: Jose Najarro Stocks
posts.text:
Advanced Micro Devices $AMD just registered up to 336.9 million shares for resale, and the headline number looks a lot scarier than it is.

Per the S-3 filed today, 320 million of those shares come from the OpenAI and Meta warrants, 160 million each at a $0.01 exercise price. They only vest in tranches as each company buys AMD Instinct GPUs, starting at the first gigawatt and fully vesting at 6 gigawatts, and they also need AMD stock price targets that climb to $600 for the final tranche. AMD is registering them under piggyback registration rights.

The rest, about 16.9 million shares, belongs to the sellers of Taalas and World Labs, the two AI startups AMD closed this month, and part of the Taalas piece is contingent.

Why it matters: this is paperwork that lets holders sell once shares exist, not a new stock sale, and AMD gets no proceeds. The real near term overhang is roughly 17 million acquisition shares. The 320 million only show up if OpenAI and Meta actually take up to 12 gigawatts of Instinct GPUs combined, and at that point most AMD holders would gladly take that dilution.

$META $NVDA $AVGO $TSM $MU

Hewlett Packard Enterprise $HPE just grew revenue 50% and guided next year far above the Street, and the stock still slipped after hours.

FY Q4 revenue was $14.55B, up 50%, vs $14.45B market consensus. Adjusted EPS was $1.43 vs $1.29 market consensus and above HPE's own $1.20 to $1.30 guide. Server revenue hit $8.8B, up 94.7%, and Cloud & AI operating margin doubled to 18.4% from 9.3%. HPE says Q4 orders grew almost 90%, faster than revenue.

The guide is the real story. Q1 revenue of $14.0B to $14.6B vs $13.09B market consensus, adjusted EPS $1.30 to $1.40 vs $1.10. FY27 revenue raised to $59.4B to $63.1B vs $55.12B market consensus, adjusted EPS $5.05 to $5.35 vs $4.74, and free cash flow of at least $5.5B. Plus another $5B of buyback authorization, about $7.3B total, and a $0.17 dividend.

"We have a perfect portfolio to capture that inflection point across networking, cloud and AI," Antonio Neri told MarketWatch, adding that memory, flash and networking supply should stay tight into the back half of 2028.

Why it matters: servers nearly doubling with orders running ahead of sales says AI server demand is still accelerating, and tight memory supply into 2028 is one more tailwind for the memory names. The after hours dip of roughly 5-6% comes after the stock ran about 17% today with the rest of AI.

posts.text:
$AMD filed an SEC registration covering the potential resale of up to 336.9M shares, including 320M tied to performance-based warrants issued to OpenAI and Meta ($META).

* OpenAI Warrants: OpenAI can acquire up to 160M AMD shares at $0.01 each, subject to GPU purchase milestones, stock-price targets and other conditions. The warrants expire in October 2030.

* Meta $META Warrants: Meta holds similar rights to 160M shares at $0.01 each, with an expiration in February 2031.

* Vesting Conditions: Both agreements tie share awards to $AMD GPU purchases reaching 6 GW for full vesting, alongside stock-price targets rising to $600 per share for the final tranche.

* Acquisition Shares: The registration also covers approximately 15M shares from AMD's World Labs acquisition and 1.96M tied to its Taalas acquisition.

* Nvidia Connection: Nvidia ($NVDA) and its subsidiary NVentures are listed for a combined 437,338 $AMD shares received through the World Labs acquisition.

* Important Distinction: This is a resale registration, not an announced sale of 336.9M shares. OpenAI and Meta's warrants remain subject to vesting and exercise conditions. AMD receives no proceeds from shareholder resales.

posts.text:
On se souviendra de cette séance pendant 10 ans

Ce qu'il faut retenir de cette séance folle :

1. Jensen revient, les shorts explosent

A/ Le board de Nvidia réintègre Jensen Huang à l'unanimité comme président, CEO et administrateur, avec effet immédiat. Colette Kress, qui assurait l'intérim, reste CFO et Harvey Jones reste chairman. Côté garde-fous, l'enquête interne continue, un comité sécurité nationale et contrôle export est mis en place et Nvidia cherche un chief compliance officer.

B/ La demande était intacte dans les chiffres, le marché rend la décote de gouvernance. Par contre, ça expose un énorme key-man risk chez Nvidia, il n'y a juste pas de plan B. Et les shorts restent encore gagnants de 14 Md$ depuis fin octobre, ils ont largement du gras pour revenir à la charge

C'est l'une des meilleur sessions de l'histoire de Wall-Street pour la tech. Lunaire après la semaine horrible

2. Ce que son retour change vraiment

Au-delà du rebond immédiat, c'est un signal fort pour tout l'écosystème IA. Le retour de Jensen redonne à Nvidia sa capacité à fédérer l'industrie, sécurise sa culture interne et rassure sur l'exécution de la roadmap produit déjà annoncée, ce qui ouvre la porte à un re-rating du multiple.   

Deux zones grises restent quand même sur la table. D'abord, rien ne garantit que Nvidia pourra continuer à monter des gros investissements multi-parties avec ses partenaires de l'écosystème à la même échelle qu'avant. Ensuite, le réglementaire reste un vrai poids sur le titre entre l'enquête du DOJ sur d'éventuelles violations de contrôle export via des clients (notamment à Singapour), la surveillance accrue dans certaines juridictions et l'enquête de la SEC sur les anciennes publications financières. 

Tant que ces dossiers ne sont pas réglés ou mieux éclaircis, cet overhang va continuer de coller au titre

2. Trump fait le deal, Bessent plie

Dans la nuit, Trump écrit qu'il espère le retour de Jensen. Ce lundi sur CNBC, il revendique carrément le coup en disant avoir parlé au board et "fait le deal", répétant que Jensen "n'a rien fait de mal". Bessent, qui exigeait un CEO externe le 15 novembre, retourne sa veste dimanche sur CBS en expliquant que Jensen est "déjà à l'extérieur". Hilarant.

On a officiellement un "Trump Put" sur Nvidia. Ça sauve le cours ce soir, mais si Washington remet Jensen sur le siège, Washington garde la laisse. En plus du DOJ et de la SEC, le FBI, la Californie et le Congrès creusent toujours, avec l'affaire Megaspeed et les 880 000 puces vers la Chine qui maintiennent Lutnick sous pression.

3. Anthropic n'est pas convié à la fête

Pendant que tout le secteur explose, la plus grosse IPO de l'histoire reste sur le bord de la route. Après +17 % jeudi et -8,5 % vendredi, $ANT recule encore de 2,8 % à 86,4 $ en séance, à peine 4 % au-dessus de son prix d'IPO à 83 $.

En effet, Dario est vue comme le gros perdant du retour de Jensen mettant en avant l'écosystème Open weight (FTW!). Sale coup pour le petit Dario et sa soeur

4. La Fed serait elle le vrai piège du jour ? 

C'est le revers de la médaille de cette séance. En faisant exploser les actions, le marché détend les conditions financières et force la main à la Fed. Les probabilités d'une hausse de 25 pb le 9 décembre grimpent ce soir à 98 %, contre 88 % vendredi, avec un 10 ans US collé vers 4,92 %.

Un taux sans risque proche de 5 %, c'est le seul vrai frein de court terme que je prends au sérieux sur les multiples tech, concernant le long terme, la vague de fond semble un peu innarrêtable

Ce que dit le Bear vs Bull

De ce que je capte l'ensemble de la street est sonnée et se demande si on tient enfin un point bas sur les semis ou juste un squeeze à revendre, pour le moment tous les rebonds étaient "bons à revendre"

A/ Côté bear, ce rebond ne règle ni le financement de l'IA, ni les enquêtes sur Nvidia, ni la hausse quasi actée de la Fed, et les shorts ont encore de quoi taper le rebond. Les plus bears parlent d'un problème sur le comp

posts.name: EndGame Macro
posts.text:
When One Man Becomes Too Important to Fail, The Entire Financial System Has A Problem

I believe Jensen Huang’s reinstatement revealed more than a leadership dispute. It exposed how dependent markets and confidence have become on NVIDIA and the AI investment cycle.

What Changed Behind Closed Doors

On November 17, NVIDIA’s board rejected Huang’s reinstatement following intelligence revelations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence connection.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent advocated replacing Huang with an outside executive and questioned NVIDIA’s export compliance culture.

Six days later, it reversed course.

Trump acknowledged personally intervening with NVIDIA’s directors. Vice President JD Vance reportedly participated, while the administration provided national security assurances supporting Huang’s return.

Bessent’s position had softened, while compliance concerns remained.

The explanation lies in the financial consequences.

The Economic Threat Became Too Large

NVIDIA reportedly lost more than $1.2 trillion in market capitalization following the scandal. Selling spread across semiconductors, data center infrastructure and broader equities.

The S&P 500 suffered seven consecutive losing sessions before Huang’s reinstatement triggered a rally. NVIDIA surged 30%, lifting technology stocks and major indices.

I find that rally more bearish than bullish.

One executive’s removal contributed to an enormous destruction of market value. His return helped reverse it almost overnight.

Yet nothing fundamentally changed in the broader economy.

Interest rates remained restrictive. Corporate credit spreads were widening, commercial real estate faced enormous refinancing pressures, household delinquencies were rising and private sector credit demand was weakening.

The violent rally likely reflected substantial repositioning and short covering alongside genuine relief, rather than a sudden improvement in economic fundamentals.

Even after collapsing nearly 27%, the VIX remained above 26.

That is not evidence of a healthy, stable market. It reveals how sensitive investor positioning and confidence had become to one individual.

National Security Meets Financial Stability

I believe Trump recognized that keeping Huang out threatened two objectives.

Preserving American technological dominance over China and preventing a disorderly collapse in confidence surrounding AI investment.

AI spending has become an important source of economic growth, supporting semiconductors, electricity infrastructure, construction and corporate capital investment.

A sustained collapse in confidence could threaten financing throughout that ecosystem.

Reinstating Huang offered an opportunity to stabilize markets without emergency monetary intervention or a direct financial rescue.

Government assurances also gave NVIDIA’s board justification to reverse course while investigations continued.

The Bigger Economic Question

I believe administration officials recognize that economic deterioration is underway and understand how vulnerable markets have become. Rather than allowing a collapse in confidence to accelerate that deterioration, they appear to be managing the timing and severity of the adjustment, preserving stability while buying time against forces they may no longer be able to reverse.

Huang’s reinstatement removed one catalyst. It did nothing to resolve the underlying vulnerabilities.

Preventing a financial collapse today does not prevent a recession tomorrow. It may buy time.

The economic and strategic consequences of keeping Huang out ultimately outweighed the risks of reinstating him.

And the market rally may be the most troubling evidence.

If restoring one executive can reverse hundreds of billions in market losses overnight, how much of America’s apparent economic resilience rests on sustainable fundamentals, and how much depends on preserving confidence in an increasingly concentrated AI investment cycle?

$MU $SKHY

3D DRAM will be a necessity for AGI and super intelligent agents because of the extreme bandwidth they need between GPU and memory.

CEO Sanjay Mehrotra: All major customers are seeking to collaborate on stacked 3D DRAM. Broader adoption expected in 2030–2031.

Initial market traction expected in 2028–2029. Despite thermal challenges, 3D DRAM could become a key growth engine toward the end of the decade.

Scott DeBoer (CTO): “Literally every big customer is asking us for partnership in developing this technology with the opportunity to co-design a base die, stack memory on top of that, and put that known good product on top of an accelerator chip. In that sense, it is really the thing that moves AI to the next level.”

On timing (DeBoer): Multi-layer stacks on processors will probably start coming into the market in 2028–2029, then grow from there. “Certainly by 2030–2031, you will see a big proliferation of this” because of the impact on AI productivity.

Thermal is a major hurdle. DRAM is temperature-sensitive and would sit directly on top of high-power GPUs/accelerators. That means managing hotspots, bonding materials, the DRAM stack, and cooling systems.

Stacked 3D DRAM requires close co-innovation with customers. This could help Micron move beyond commodity-driven pricing toward a more strategic role in AI system design and deeper ties with major AI players.

Related notes from the summit:

75% of Micron’s 2027 supply is already sold out; discussions now moving into 2028
26 Strategic Customer Agreements (SCAs) backed by $32 billion in upfront cash and financial commitments

posts.text:
A few thoughts on what I saw and heard at the @TomorrowXSummit:

1) As many others have noted, cautious and bearish views on the AI trade abounded at the conference among institutional investors (tech people and individual investors were often more bullish). But while I heard a slew of bearish arguments, I thought only two really carried weight given the massive capex cuts priced in by current valuations:

A) That recent $ANT inference revenue and compute estimates suggest we’ll need far fewer GW of compute than what’s currently set to be built.

B) That the recent slowdown in frontier lab ARR growth suggests we won’t see enough revenue generated to justify planned capex.

I think the first argument often relies on questionable numbers – for example, a belief that Anthropic only needs 500MW in inference capacity to produce $100B in revenue, when they might actually be using 1.2-1.3GW today to achieve $80B in gross ARR. And more importantly, it glosses over Anthropic dedicating over 60% of its compute to training -- and why that number might not decline much, if at all, in 2027 -- and why revenue/inference GW numbers probably look very different for rival frontier labs and open-weight models (for its part, OpenAI might be relying on over 2GW in inference to produce ~$70B in gross ARR).

The second bear argument is stronger IMO given that capex might be around $1.5T next year and coding-related growth is slowing down. That said, I think fixating on Q4 OAI/Ant ARR growth overlooks:

A) How OAI/Ant appear to make up just 25-30% of non-China AI compute consumption, after accounting for open-weight and rival proprietary models, internal AI usage among the tech giants, Internet firms and ISVs, local AI deployments, etc.

B) How much (judging by data from OpenRouter, Fireworks, etc.) open-weight token consumption has exploded this year (looks like it’s up well over 10x Y/Y).

C) How early we appear to be in the adoption curve for many non-coding workloads (knowledge/enterprise work, cyber, R&D, etc.).

D) How OAI/Ant’s compute commitments, balance sheets and LLM progress make them unlikely to meaningfully change their capex plans in response to a quarter or two of slow ARR growth.

E) What the cloud giants are both reporting quarterly as well as signaling for the next couple of years ($AMZN guiding for 40%+ AWS growth in both 2027 and 2028, after having previously never guided more than a quarter out, seems especially notable).

F) How past capex booms (railroads, factories, fiber, etc.) typically ended only after years of supply/capacity being well ahead of demand, rather than after supply got just moderately ahead of demand (and of course, even that’s not the case right now).

Meanwhile, though I heard plenty of bearish arguments, I got less pushback than I thought I would for various bullish arguments (related to token/cloud growth, GPU prices, future non-coding adoption, LLM progress, etc.). That, together with all the non-fundamental reasons I heard and overheard for wanting to avoid AI infra (e.g. wanting to lock in gains for the year, not wanting to risk underperforming peers/benchmarks, etc.), made me think a lot of the negativity we’ve seen lately comes from investors being frightened/unsettled by recent price action and thus trying to rationalize that price action ex-post, much as we saw with SaaS and Internet stocks earlier this year.

2) The optimism from people closely monitoring LLM progress about major advances happening next year was notable. I heard multiple predictions that RSI would be achieved next year (one could argue the labs have already achieved partial RSI – see METR’s recent report on the pace of Anthropic LLM advances), as well as that LLMs capable of fully generalizing across robotics tasks/environments would arrive in 2027.

• Quantum arithmetic: 290x lower resource costs

posts.text:
CrowdStrike is buying Zscaler for $43.9B in stock.

It's the largest cybersecurity acquisition on record.

Three things stood out to me:

1️⃣ CrowdStrike buys the network security it was missing.

CrowdStrike started as the leader in endpoint security.

SASE, which secures every connection between users, agents and apps, is one of its few gaps.

Zscaler is a leader in SASE, one of the most attractive areas of cyber in the agentic AI era.

As CrowdStrike put it: "The endpoint is where the agent runs. The network is where it goes."

Palo Alto Networks says agentic traffic on its SASE network grew ~9x in a year.

2️⃣ The products fit, and I think the synergies are easy to achieve.

The two already sell side by side: 2,000+ shared customers across 16 integrations.

Both are founder-led, with complementary cultures.

~8,000 Zscaler customers don't use CrowdStrike yet.

The targets: $1B in revenue synergies and $500M in cost synergies.

George Kurtz is well respected within Zscaler and in the cyber space more broadly.

Demonstrating great leadership through tough times...

It had nearly doubled this year, and shareholders don't want the incremental risk.

The company has generally grown more organically, especially compared to Palo Alto.

But by our math, CrowdStrike is paying ~11x Zscaler's ARR, with stock valued at ~39x its own.

posts.text:
I'm thrilled to announce CrowdStrike has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Zscaler. This is a big day for @CrowdStrike, @Zscaler, our customers, and the cybersecurity market.

We’re doing this coming off the best quarter in company history: all-time record net new ARR of $419M, up 58%, ending ARR accelerating for the fifth consecutive quarter, all-time record free cash flow of $474M, and a raise to our FY27 net new ARR guidance. For the first time, security is the gas pedal, not the brake.

AI is the greatest sea change I've seen in my lifetime. Every enterprise is deploying AI. And they tell us: We don't know where our AI agents are. We don't know what they're doing. What data are they touching? Where are they going on the network?

Falcon Guardian answers those questions on the device and in the cloud. On the network? That's Zscaler. Together, we'll secure AI on the device, in the cloud, and across the network in between.

THE MAST DISCLOSURE: WHAT THE BIS LICENSE RECORDS ACTUALLY SHOW

On November 19, 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, chaired by Rep. Brian Mast, publicly released Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) export license application information for NVIDIA and AMD AI chip sales to China. The release is stronger and weaker than the headline at the same time: stronger, because the government's own license table puts the Megaspeed channel's entities inside NVIDIA's applications, including one direct application to a Megaspeed-network company; weaker, because the same table shows zero shipments against the approvals as of May 11, 2026, the two largest asks returned without action, and only previous-generation chips throughout.

WHAT WAS RELEASED, AND UNDER WHAT AUTHORITY

• The legal vehicle is the Export Control Reform Act disclosure provision, 50 U.S.C. 4820(h)(2)(B)(ii): the committee determined that withholding the information is contrary to the national interest. The underlying BIS table is marked CUI//SP-EXPT, statutorily protected export information, releasable only on that determination.

posts.text:
I’ve always thought that @CeoOndas and the rest of the $ONDS team were great communicators, and this only proves that point further.

This shareholder letter addresses many investor concerns, especially those around further dilution and whether or not the acquisition spree will continue.

It seems like investors need not be worried about either of those:

“Our existing portfolio now provides a foundation for substantial continued growth without requiring additional acquisitions.

That is an important milestone. The rapid expansion of Ondas has required considerable investment; our priority is to translate this scale into even stronger financial performance. We are focused on expanding margins, deepening integration, increasing operating efficiency, and achieving our Adjusted EBITDA profitability objectives as revenue grows.”

“… We intend to substantially moderate the pace of new acquisitions and maintain a particularly high threshold for deploying capital into additional businesses.”

“We will only consider using equity as acquisition currency when we believe that relative valuation and transaction economics are exceptionally attractive.”

This is exactly what many of us wanted to hear and it’s obvious $ONDS leadership has a finger on the pulse of retail investors as well as Wall Street.

A dedicated focus on execution comes next:

“As we look toward 2027, our priorities are straightforward: execute against customer demand and backlog, accelerate deployment of our technologies, continue to innovate, strengthen operating capabilities, improve margins and cash generation, and allocate capital with discipline.”

“We have spent the past several years building the Ondas platform. Our next chapter is about realizing and compounding its full economic potential.”

Well done Eric! Very excited for what comes next. 👏

$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE *NVIDIA BOARD REINSTATES JENSEN HUANG AS CEO

NVIDIA Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as President, CEO and Board Director
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 23, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.
The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.
For further information, contact:

$NVDA NVIDIA OPTIONS POSITIONING AFTER THE SELLOFF

THE SETUP

• Friday's close was $125.53, 47.5% below the trailing 12-month closing high. Monday's premarket print in this data is $136.68, up $11.15, +8.9%, a headline-driven bounce into the open.
• What follows is Bloomberg option expiration data: open interest as of Friday's close, delta notional by strike and expiry, measured at the $136.68 print. Open interest shows the size and the sign of the delta in the complex. It does not show who holds it.

THE SHORT DELTA IS IN THE PUTS

• The put book alone carries -$49B of delta notional. About -$39B of it sits above 115% moneyness, strikes of roughly $157 and higher: deep in-the-money puts, not overhead call supply. The 130-150% band, strikes of about $178 to $205, is -$12.4B, and above 150% there is another -$15.6B, about -$28B in total above the $178 line.
• It is concentrated in the near columns: the 1-month put column is -$10.3B and the 2-month column is -$10.7B, about -$21B between them.
• In-the-money put delta is largely mechanical. With the strike above spot, delta runs near -1 per contract, and as spot rises toward those strikes the delta bleeds off on its own. A rally shrinks this overhang instead of running into it.

THE CALL BOOK IS NET LONG

• The combined book, calls and puts together, totals -$23.6B. Calls alone are therefore net long about +$25.4B of delta (combined minus puts). There is no written call wall in these screens.
• Above 130% moneyness, calls alone are net positive about +$11.3B: +$3.9B in the $178 to $205 band and +$7.4B above it. Calls alone are also positive in the near columns, +$5.8B in the 1-month column and +$3.8B in the 2-month column.
• The band just overhead, 110-120% moneyness at strikes of about $150 to $164, is -$5.9B combined, and the split matters: that is puts at -$8.8B against calls at +$2.9B. It is put delta, not call supply.

BELOW SPOT

• Outright put protection below spot is thin. The put book below 90% moneyness totals only about -$2.0B.
• The combined book below 90% moneyness is +$4.4B, but that is deep in-the-money call delta, not downside hedging. At strikes under 50% moneyness in the 1-month column, puts are just -$54M against about +$947M of calls. This book is not heavily hedged for a fresh leg down either.

THE READ

• Net, the entire NVIDIA options complex is short about $23.6B of delta, and the centre of gravity is mechanical in-the-money put delta that decays as spot rises toward the strikes. Strength erodes the short-delta overhang rather than feeding a wall of written calls, because there is no wall in these screens.
• The repricing is visible between this morning's two prints. The same open interest measured at the $134.94 premarket print was -$50.8B in puts and -$26B combined; at $136.68 it is -$49B in puts and -$23.6B combined. Open interest has not changed, because it is Friday's close; the delta is repricing as spot rises, so the bleed-off is already showing up in the screens.
• It cuts both ways. With only about $2.0B of put delta below 90% moneyness, the options book is not positioned to cushion a renewed selloff. The positioning argues for a bounce that gets easier as it climbs, and a break lower that meets little options-book support.
• What would change the read: the in-the-money put block above $178 being closed or rolled down, or real put buying appearing below spot. Until one of those prints, the bounce is working against a shrinking overhang, not a fixed ceiling.

Great revenue & operating income projections for $ONDS looking ahead to 2027 and beyond (Peter’s post below).

$ONDS (stock) has no doubt struggled this year, along with every other high beta name - without exception.

But I believe the underlying business is fundamentally better positioned than the vast majority of other high beta names out there.

People have lots of opinions about $ONDS’s management and whether or not they’re executing. For me, it’s hard to say they’re not doing a great job in such a small amount of time.

12-18 months ago they were a small wireless communications company that had just announced a bold plan to evolve into a major defense tech firm, and had just begun acquiring the companies needed to do so.

Already, that acquisition spree has been proven largely successful and half a dozen of their new subsidiaries are showing fantastic organic growth rates.

Retail investors are incredibly impatient, however, so when the entire defense sector fell dramatically this year (along with space, quantum, rare earths, nuclear, solar, robotics, etc… and finally AI), criticisms have been rampant across FinX.

I suppose Eric & team should have evolved into a successful defense prime that was growing revenues in the triple digits (or more) and became EBITDA positive in a single year instead of the projected ~2 years.

In the grand scheme of things, this is ridiculous.

Investing can’t, and won’t, always be fast money, all the time.

The Political Battle Over AI and The Fight To Control America’s Economic Future Before 2028

On September 13, I examined the convergence of political interests, corporate incentives and calls to slow AI development. On November 3, I discussed how an economic crisis could reshape AI policy. On November 11, I questioned the timing of the intelligence revelations surrounding Jensen Huang.

Following Huang’s reinstatement, Hakeem Jeffries is demanding investigations into NVIDIA, Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce, alongside stronger semiconductor export restrictions.

The Political Groundwork

In December 2025, Jeffries established the House Democratic Commission on AI and the Innovation Economy.

In September, Obama privately encouraged making AI central to the Democratic agenda, while Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Elon Musk expressed support for stronger AI oversight.

Democrats had reason to anticipate a strong midterm performance and develop their governing agenda before assuming congressional control.

On October 29, Democratic lawmakers introduced a resolution opposing taxpayer bailouts following an AI collapse. Valerie Foushee, a leader of Jeffries’s AI commission, was a sponsor.

That same day, the Huang intelligence revelations became public, 5 days before the midterms.

The Intelligence Disclosure

Trump was reportedly briefed in 2025, while Rubio oversaw an intelligence assessment in spring 2026.

My post examined 2 possibilities.

•    Individuals with access to classified intelligence strategically disclosed the information for political leverage.

•    Chinese intelligence sacrificed a potentially compromised relationship to destabilize American AI leadership and semiconductor policy.

Neither theory has been established. Why intelligence reportedly known for months surfaced immediately before the election deserves scrutiny.

Democrats subsequently secured a decisive electoral victory and will gain greater congressional investigative authority in January.

The Economic And Political Collision

Huang’s resignation intensified technology losses and institutional deleveraging. His reinstatement restored approximately $950 billion in NVIDIA market capitalization.

Persistent energy disruptions threaten corporate profitability and household purchasing power. Credit conditions are deteriorating while AI infrastructure commitments face uncertainty surrounding future returns.

Congressional investigations could examine AI financing, private credit, export licensing, electricity costs, corporate relationships and employment displacement.

Established AI companies could benefit from regulatory requirements that smaller competitors struggle to afford.

Political and corporate interests could therefore converge around the same regulatory agenda without any coordinated effort to engineer a market collapse.

The Battle Over What Comes After

If a severe recession develops in 2027, disagreements over corporate bailouts, household relief, AI regulation and responsibility for economic losses could dominate Washington.

Democratic congressional control could influence that response.

Persistent energy inflation could delay monetary easing. Even when rate cuts begin, monetary policy cannot restore energy supplies or make unprofitable AI investments economically viable.

The broader benefits for employment, consumption and investment could take 18 to 24 months or longer to materialize.

If easing begins in 2027, meaningful recovery might not arrive until 2028 or 2029, carrying significant electoral consequences.

Politicians do not need to manufacture an economic crisis to influence its consequences. Huang’s reinstatement may have temporarily stabilized the AI trade, but the larger battle over who regulates the industry, who absorbs its potential losses and who receives credit for the eventual economic recovery may only be beginning.

Are Wall Street’s Largest Hedge Funds Being Forced To Liquidate Precious Metals?

The recent precious metals selloff may have less to do with fundamentals and more to do with institutional deleveraging.

I would be closely monitoring Millennium Management, Balyasny Asset Management, Rokos Capital and Marshall Wace, all of which suffered reported losses in October.

The Pressure Was Building Before Huang Resigned

Reported October fund performance

•   Millennium Management declined 2.3%.

•   Balyasny Asset Management declined 3.4%.

•   Rokos Capital declined 4.9%.

•   Marshall Wace Eureka declined 5.4%.

Millennium was reportedly withdrawing more than $1.5 billion from external managers following losses.

September SEC filings also revealed substantial NVIDIA common stock holdings across these managers.

•   Marshall Wace held $3.44 billion.

•   Millennium held $2.98 billion.

•   Balyasny held $1.13 billion.

•   Rokos held $530 million.

Combined exposure exceeded $8 billion in common stock, excluding derivatives.

These positions may have changed, and disclosed options and undisclosed hedges could offset losses. Nevertheless, the scale of their involvement warrants attention.

Following Jensen Huang’s resignation on November 12, the technology selloff intensified. Global hedge funds reportedly lost approximately 4% in November through the 20th, with Goldman Sachs identifying aggressive deleveraging.

If these four funds experienced comparable November losses, their cumulative drawdowns could range from approximately 6% to 9% since October began.

The Prime Brokerage Connection

All four managers have documented prime brokerage relationships with affiliates of JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley.

These institutions provide financing, securities lending, derivatives services and access to leverage.

When volatility increases and portfolio values decline, prime brokers can increase collateral requirements and reduce available leverage. Funds also face internal risk limits that can force portfolio managers to unwind positions.

Relatively modest capital losses can therefore trigger disproportionately large reductions in market exposure.

Why Gold And Silver Could Become Collateral Damage

SEC filings also reveal gold related holdings and derivatives exposure at Millennium, Balyasny and Marshall Wace, while Rokos disclosed exposure to gold miners.

If losses elsewhere create liquidity needs, these institutions could sell precious metals regardless of their fundamental outlook.

Elevated financing costs, dollar appreciation and correlated positioning could amplify the pressure.

We witnessed similar dynamics in 2008 and March 2020, when even traditionally defensive assets were liquidated as institutions scrambled for cash.

Why The Liquidation May Not Be Over

I suspect Huang’s resignation accelerated a deleveraging process that was already underway rather than initiating it.

His reinstatement may relieve immediate market pressure, but it does not automatically reverse accumulated losses, restore leverage allowances or eliminate collateral requirements.

There is no confirmation that these specific funds are responsible for precious metals selling or that their prime brokers issued margin calls.

Nevertheless, their disclosed exposures, reported losses and broader industry deleveraging make them worth monitoring.

The biggest mistake investors could make is confusing speculative selling exhaustion with the end of systemic deleveraging. When institutions need dollars, what they believe an asset is worth becomes secondary to how quickly they can sell it.

Bill Ackman Sounds The Alarm On A Federal Reserve Policy That Could Deepen America’s Economic And Debt Crisis

Bill Ackman @BillAckman raises a warning about a Federal Reserve rate increase on December 9. I share his concern that policymakers may be underestimating the deterioration occurring while relying on headline growth and employment figures.

His argument that geopolitical instability, inflationary pressures and changing economic conditions warrant monetary policy flexibility deserves consideration.

Financial Conditions Are Already Tightening

The rising cost of capital is becoming difficult for businesses to absorb. SpaceX secured financing at 8.259%.

Banks report weakening loan demand and tighter lending standards. Household debt reached $19.1 trillion, with 5% in some stage of delinquency.

Small business Subchapter V bankruptcies increased 43% through October, while approximately $875 billion in commercial mortgages face maturities in 2026.

Meanwhile, GDP benefits from government spending and concentrated AI investment, even as weakness spreads throughout other areas of the economy.

Unemployment near 4.2% fails to capture reduced working hours, discouraged workers, involuntary part time employment and hiring freezes.

Businesses typically reduce investment and hiring before deteriorating profitability forces layoffs.

The Inflation Problem Monetary Policy Cannot Resolve

Geopolitical instability, tariffs, deglobalization, military expenditures and massive AI infrastructure requirements are creating structural inflationary pressures.

These developments do not necessarily reflect excessive consumer demand.

Diesel refining margins near $80 per barrel despite declining crude prices illustrate how supply constraints can sustain elevated costs throughout transportation, agriculture and manufacturing.

Higher interest rates cannot repair refineries, restore shipping routes or increase electricity generation.

They can, however, discourage the investment necessary to address these shortages.

This creates a dangerous policy dilemma. Inflation remains elevated partly because supply is constrained, while monetary tightening weakens the investment and economic activity needed to expand productive capacity.

The Federal Debt and Demographic Constraint

Gross federal debt exceeds 120% of GDP, while publicly held debt approaches 100%.

Reducing these ratios requires debt to grow more slowly than nominal GDP, not necessarily repaying outstanding obligations.

But America’s demographic trajectory makes generating sufficient real economic growth difficult.

The BLS projects annual labor force growth of just 0.3% through 2035, while population aging increases retirement and health care obligations.

AI and automation could improve productivity, but capital expenditures do not automatically translate into widespread economic efficiency.

Higher inflation could increase nominal GDP and reduce the relative burden of existing debt. However, higher inflation expectations could also increase Treasury yields as debt matures.

Persistent primary deficits complicate the arithmetic, even if inflation settles near 3%.

The Bigger Economic Risk

Financial conditions can continue tightening without additional Fed increases. Real borrowing costs rise when inflation expectations decline while nominal rates remain elevated, and a stronger dollar and widening credit spreads create restraint.

Meanwhile, deteriorating household credit, business restructurings and commercial real estate refinancing pressures reveal vulnerabilities that headline economic indicators may not fully capture.

My concern is that monetary policy remains restrictive until credit losses, refinancing failures and unemployment begin reinforcing one another. By then, the economy could already be experiencing a self sustaining contraction, leaving the Federal Reserve responding to economic damage that accumulated long before it became visible in the headline data.

The cost of equity capital has also increased materially with the recent substantial decline in the stock market. 

The Fed’s 2% inflation ambition is misguided. Geopolitical risk and the required investment in global military spending, de globalization and tariffs, and the massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set. 3% inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world. 

The Fed will put the U.S. and world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%.

posts.text:
Gold and silver may be approaching selling exhaustion but I am considerably less convinced that the broader liquidation cycle has ended.

Gold recently declined approximately 12%, while silver lost roughly 21%. Despite rebounding 4% and 5% today, they recovered only 29% and 19% of their previous losses.

Recent positioning data also suggest substantial speculative selling has occurred, with silver’s net speculative long position reportedly falling to just 17 contracts.

That supports the possibility of a near term bottom, but speculative liquidation and systemic deleveraging are two entirely different things.

Claims of backwardation, if sustained and verified, could indicate unusually strong demand for immediate physical delivery. However, physical scarcity does not guarantee rising prices when financial institutions are forced to raise liquidity.

During 2008 and March 2020, precious metals experienced significant liquidation despite their appeal as monetary safe havens.

When institutions need cash to meet margin calls, repay debt or reduce leverage, they sell what they can, not necessarily what they want to.

The Bigger Warning Is Coming From Credit and Currency Markets

The Dollar Index above 104, elevated real interest rates, widening credit spreads among weaker borrowers and deteriorating private sector lending conditions suggest financial pressures remain substantial.

I believe we may be transitioning from an inflationary economic cycle toward a much more dangerous credit and balance sheet adjustment.

As leveraged positions unwind, demand for dollars can increase, strengthening the currency and placing additional pressure on international borrowers.

That creates the potential for another wave of forced asset sales, regardless of how attractive precious metals appear fundamentally.

The Refining Market Is Revealing Another Economic Vulnerability

The latest refining data make this situation even more concerning.

The benchmark U.S. crack spread has fallen from approximately $72 per barrel in September to $41, suggesting the extreme refining squeeze is easing.

But beneath that decline, diesel refining margins remain near $80 per barrel, compared with approximately $20 for gasoline.

Diesel margins are roughly four times higher, while distillate inventories remain approximately 15% below their five year average.

That divergence matters.

Falling crude and gasoline margins could reflect improving supply, weakening demand or both. Yet persistent diesel shortages continue raising costs throughout transportation, agriculture, manufacturing and distribution.

Businesses could therefore experience weakening revenue growth while essential operating costs remain elevated.

That combination compresses profitability, discourages investment and eventually threatens employment.

It also complicates the Federal Reserve’s ability to ease monetary policy if inflation remains elevated despite deteriorating economic activity.

Why I Believe Another Liquidation Wave Remains Possible

Silver is particularly vulnerable because weakening industrial activity could compound selling driven by financial deleveraging.

I have greater confidence in gold establishing a durable bottom, but even gold is not immune to a systemic liquidity shock.

A broader dollar funding crisis has not been confirmed, and stabilizing financial conditions could support a substantial recovery in precious metals.

Nevertheless, my concern is that speculative selling may be nearing completion while the larger global deleveraging process is only beginning.

The critical question is not whether investors have finished selling gold and silver because they no longer want them. It is whether the global financial system has finished selling assets because it needs dollars.

Given restrictive real rates, weakening credit conditions, mounting refinancing pressures and persistent energy distortions, I believe another liquidation phase remains a serious possibility.

The Dollar’s Relentless Rise May Be Signaling The Beginning Of A Global Deleveraging Crisis

I believe the dollar’s extraordinary strength reflects something far more consequential than expectations for another Federal Reserve rate hike. The global financial system may be transitioning from an inflation problem toward a credit and balance sheet problem as restrictive monetary conditions collide with weakening growth.

What Robin Brooks’s Chart Reveals

@robin_j_brooks shows the dollar accelerating against G10 currencies while America’s forward interest rate advantage has failed to keep pace.

That divergence matters. When the dollar rises without a corresponding increase in relative yields, something beyond conventional monetary policy expectations is driving demand.

What I think is happening is that elevated real interest rates, defensive capital flows and the unwinding of leveraged international positions are driving the dollar higher.

ING recently reported U.S. 2 year real swap rates exceeding 2.4%, approaching their highest levels since 2023.

When inflation expectations decline faster than nominal rates, real borrowing costs increase even without additional Fed tightening.

The Global Deleveraging Mechanism

Brooks also identified dollar strength against emerging market currencies consistent with carry trade unwinding. Speculative dollar positioning reportedly reached levels comparable to the European sovereign debt crisis.

When investors liquidate foreign assets to repay dollar funding, they purchase dollars. That strengthens the currency, increases pressure on unhedged foreign borrowers and can force further liquidations.

The process becomes self reinforcing.

Dollar appreciation pressures emerging market currencies, tightens financial conditions and weakens global economic activity.

Meanwhile, corporate credit spreads are widening, commercial real estate faces enormous refinancing pressures, business loan demand is weakening and labor market momentum is deteriorating.

The dollar becomes both a symptom of financial stress and a mechanism that intensifies it.

Why Geopolitics Makes This More Dangerous

Energy disruptions involving Iran and the Strait of Hormuz introduce another layer of pressure.

Even as crude declines, expensive refined fuels can sustain inflation throughout transportation, agriculture and manufacturing.

Energy importing economies face additional financial strain while relatively elevated American real yields attract international capital.

The dollar may therefore strengthen not because America is becoming healthier, but because conditions elsewhere are deteriorating faster.

Consider what happened today...

NVIDIA surged following Huang’s reinstatement, technology stocks rallied and the VIX collapsed. Yet the dollar remained exceptionally strong.

That suggests forces extending beyond daily equity market sentiment.

The Federal Reserve’s Growing Policy Trap

A systemic dollar shortage is not yet confirmed. Funding markets have not demonstrated the extreme dislocations associated with 2008 or March 2020.

But the Fed risks underestimating monetary tightening already occurring through real yields, credit deterioration and international currency markets.

It may not need to raise rates again for financial conditions to become substantially more restrictive.

I suspect that the dollar is beginning to reflect defensive capital flows and deleveraging rather than simply superior American economic prospects.

The warning is that the dollar may be rising not because the United States is becoming stronger, but because the global financial system is becoming less capable of sustaining the leverage accumulated during the expansion.

posts.name: Jeffrey Currie 🆔++
posts.text:
The Fed cannot fight FED.

I joined @FerroTV on @business this morning to raise three important points. 

The first: Gold lost 15% in nine trading days and is up 4% today. Both moves are liquidity. In a squeeze you sell what you can, not what you want, and gold bounced the day the forced selling stopped. 

Today's rally came from Nvidia's boardroom, not from the Fed. A December hike is still priced. This ends when the Fed turns, and the Fed is likely to turn before a January hike, if not sooner. 

The US economy is becoming asset-heavy: AI investment is a third of growth, and it is built with borrowed money. Business spending on equipment and structures is up 1.2 points of GDP since 2021. CoreWeave pays 16% for money. That constraint already binds. A funding spike in 2025 was enough to end QT.

The second point was Oil. I call it Schrödinger's Strait: neither open nor closed. Last week, transits through Hormuz fell 15% and seven tankers were hit. The barrels that get through are expensive barrels, and that holds the floor. Enough of them get through to cap it. So Brent is a range, $85 to $100, and at $90 today it is near the bottom of it. 

We took profits before the midterms and are putting a toe back in. The key is carry and equities: a backwardated curve pays you to hold the barrel, the drillers rebuild the system, and the Munificent 7 oil majors pay you cash.

And third:  FED is Fragmentation, Electrification and Debasement, the three forces behind our supercycle call since 2020. A rate hike reopens no strait and rebuilds no supply chain (Fragmentation). It makes the grid dearer to build (Electrification). It raises the interest bill on a deficit that already pays for guns and butter (Debasement). 

These forces keep commodity prices elevated whatever the Fed does. Higher rates do little to them. However, they hurt an increasingly asset-heavy US economy.

Bear Markets are markets that go down a little on most days and go up sharply on good news, or perceived good news…

Bull Markets are markets that go up a little on most days and go down sharply on bad news, or perceived bad news…

quoted.text:
Historically, trading days where the SPX closed up more than 5% (73 times across its full history since 1928) have almost all been concentrated in major financial crises, geopolitical or macro black swans, or violent short squeezes during primary bear market downtrends, and have never occurred during low-volatility, steady bull market uptrends. 

Across all 24 occurrences of single-day gains ≥ 5% in modern US equities since 1950, the following day (T+1) has typically seen profit-taking and mean-reverting pullbacks. 

The index closed lower the next day 16 times (66.7%) and higher only 8 times (33.3%), with a mean next-day return of -0.81% (median -0.55%) across all 24 samples.

Here's what I do.  You decide if it's useful.  There is a level of change in my wealth that I find to be 1) absolute noise.  There is a level I find 2) slightly annoying.  A level I find that 3) pisses me off but doesn't upset me.  A level that that cause me to 4) loose sleep. A level that causes me to 5)  act to ease the pain.  Those are personal to me.  But I assure you everyone has levels like this.  I have learned that 4 and 5 are not something I am willing to experience.  I have and I don't want to again. So I operate somewhere in the range of 3-4.  Which for me place me at a risk target that I can manage and I acccept the expected return that it provides.

The stock is soaring today on the news, but he says people will eventually stop trading headlines and look harder at valuations, China risk, and whether anyone can trust Huang as the face of the company. He frames it as a national-security problem that can’t be fully buried—bigger than crypto scandals or the short-term market swings Trump reacts to. 

In Gasparino’s analysis, the administration hitched its wagon to Huang, and that’s a decision that could meaningfully damage it.

Love Huang’s reinstatement or hate it, his argument is worth hearing.

posts.text:
This morning’s rally may look impressive, but this is exactly why I covered the shorts. The market had gotten oversold enough to produce a rip-your-face-off rally. After capturing nearly 7R on the downside, there was no reason to overstay the trade.
That said, keep this morning’s action in perspective. A number of stocks are up a whopping 10%-30%, but most are barely a blip on the charts. For now, they’re counter-trend rallies in stocks that are still in significant downtrends, particularly in Technology.
The S&P 500 fell 11.6% from its October 6 record high, the first 10% correction since the February-April 2025 selloff, but we are not out of the woods. There’s still work to do before we can say an effective bottom is in place. One strong day doesn’t suddenly create a new uptrend.
For now, I expect volatility to remain elevated. Enjoy the rally, but keep it in context. The market still has to prove itself. Prepare for backing and filling, and even lower lows in the major indexes before this correction is over.
The tricky thing about an oversold market is that it can always get more oversold. And even after momentum bottoms, price can still go on to make lower lows while divergences develop. 
What I want to see now is whether this rally can last more than a day or two and broaden out beyond the most beaten-down stocks. That would increase the odds that a sustainable year-end rally can develop. If it can’t, then what we’re seeing is probably just short covering with more selling still to come.
Stronger signals have come from upside breadth thrust signals than downside oversold readings. For example, returns after 10:1 upside volume days have been higher than after big downside volume days. An even stronger message would come from two 10:1 up days without an intervening 10:1 down day. It pays to wait for upside confirmation.
A follow-through day (+1% on higher d/d volume) could occur as early as this Friday, assuming Friday’s lows hold. That would be an initial step in determining a low has been made.
During corrections, my focus ultimately turns to individual stocks and market leadership. Currently, our list of potential candidates is small. A market cannot carry itself very far on the backs of counter trend rallies in broken leaders. To get bullish, we need to see more.  http://minervini.com

Bret Taylor has done almost everything in business and tech, from creating Google Maps to becoming Facebook's CTO to co-running Salesforce and now chairing OpenAI.

But there is one thing Taylor has never done, and which he says matters more than anything.

“I think the greatest achievement for an entrepreneur,” he told Reid Hoffman in 2024, “is to create a company and a brand that outlives you.”

Taylor’s first two startups, FriendFeed and Quip, were sold. Then shut down by their buyers.

His third and most recent business, Sierra, builds AI agents for large businesses to talk with their customers. He started it at 42 with his old friend Clay Bavor. Today, in a new announcement, it's being valued at over $30 billion, making Sierra the furthest Taylor has ever taken a company of his own.

So @domcooke called on Taylor at Sierra's office in San Francisco to ask whether it's easier or harder than ever to build a company that lasts, why every one of Taylor's co-founders has come from Google, and whether Sierra might complete his journey as an entrepreneur.

They also discussed his teenage years as a roadie for a ska band, how companies can differentiate in a world of agent-to-agent commerce, and how to make drinking cool again.

Enjoy this Q&A with one of the great elder statesmen of Silicon Valley, Bret Taylor.

quoted.text:
Here’s why the “Chief AI Officer” of Meta is wrong.

LLMs are not trained on intelligence. They are trained on the digitized output of intelligence.

The reason math and code work well for LLMs is they are self-contained verifiable domains. The artifacts of solving the problem show the work involved in reaching the solution. All of the information necessary to interpolate new combinations of existing rules already exists in the data.

That’s not true for anything else. All an LLM can do is search for patterns in the output of science, humanities, economics, and “AI research.” To go outside purely abstract verifiable domains, you need to have contact with the real world to figure out if your solution is correct or your improvement is better.

That’s why a chatbot can sort of solve the hardest math problems known to man but still just makes shit up about everything else.

LLMs are an interesting experiment that has been turned into the biggest economic mistake in U.S. history. The evidence is all around us. AI has neither created nor eliminated jobs. It has produced no groundbreaking science. It has produced no software innovations. It has generated no profits.

It is a search engine for stolen data. It is not magic beans or a god.

posts.name: jeroen blokland
posts.text:
A 3% primary surplus for 30 years?

Outgoing French President Macron has floated the idea (again) of writing budget discipline into the constitution.

It may sound promising, at least for French government bond spreads. In reality, enforcing such discipline would likely provoke enormous social and political unrest.

To prevent debt from rising further from its current 120% of GDP, France would need a primary surplus of roughly 1%. To bring debt down to the 60% threshold enshrined in the Maastricht Treaty, it would need a primary surplus of at least 3% of GDP. And even then, it would take 30 years of that surplus to reach the 60% threshold.

And that is before taking into account interest expenses, which are projected to rise by 2,5% of GDP in the next 10 years. Without offsetting measures, that means even larger deficits. For 2027 and 2028, France is already expected to run deficits well above 5% of GDP.

In addition, France has one of the world's most expensive welfare systems, with social spending exceeding 30% of GDP. As the French population ages, that share will only grow. Add defense, energy, healthcare, and everything needed to restore competitiveness and growth, and the pressure on public finances is enormous. Deficits approaching 10% of GDP are far more realistic than a balanced budget, let alone a surplus.

Achieving a sustained primary surplus would require a combination of significantly higher taxes, already among the highest in the world, and deep cuts to public spending. That means confronting the welfare state, including politically explosive measures such as raising the retirement age to something like 70. After what we have seen in recent months, the French are unlikely to simply accept that. The social and political consequences would be devastating.

Macron's constitutional budget rule, Mélenchon's call to cancel French debt held by the ECB, and Le Pen's promise to return debt to 60% of GDP are all aimed at one thing: lowering interest expenses.

None resolves the fundamental conflict between fiscal sustainability and political reality. The economic and political consequences of implementing these proposals would be enormous.

Which brings us back to the “easiest” route heavily indebted governments have repeatedly taken: artificially low interest rates and higher inflation.
For politicians, that is a much easier path to sustaining the debt burden.

For savers and bondholders, it is another story.

posts.name: Paola Rojas 🐝
posts.text: COMEX copper stocks may be effectively flowing out of the US, and explain $5.5/lb

quoted.text:
As noted earlier, Trump's tariff threat created an arbitrage opportunity in copper, sending prices soaring as it pulled an enormous amount of metal into US warehouses before the duties could take effect.

That left the rest of the world, and China in particular, short of supply.

On top of that came a flood of financial capital, drawn to copper as a key input for AI infrastructure.

Bloomberg now reports that the copper scarcity narrative has lost steam since the US midterms, as the tariffs never arrived and, following the latest electoral rebuke of Trump (which weakened figures such as Lutnick), even the biggest bulls see new levies as less likely.

So it seems that the base case has shifted away, leaving a decidedly bearish outlook.

The market is now weighing what happens if the "sea" of copper piled up in the US flows back out: the global market would be comfortably supplied, and the scarcity that had been propping up prices would disappear.

The recent selloff in AI stocks and shifting expectations for further interest-rate hikes have also added another layer of pressure on industrial metals.

#Copper
